'''Norman Julius '''"'''Boomer'''"''' Esiason''' ({{IPAc-en|ə|ˈ|s|aɪ|.|ə|s|ən}}; born April 17, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons, primarily with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland Terrapins]] and was selected in the second round of the [[1984 NFL draft]] by the Bengals, where he spent 10 seasons. Esiason was also a member of the [[New York Jets]] and [[Arizona Cardinals]].

Esiason's most successful season was in 1988 when he won [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|NFL Most Valuable Player]] (MVP) and led the Bengals to an appearance in [[Super Bowl XXIII]], which ended in a close defeat. He was also named to four [[Pro Bowl]]s and one first-team [[All-Pro]]. After nine years in Cincinnati, Esiason spent three seasons with the Jets and one season with the Cardinals before returning to the Bengals for his final season in 1997.

Since retiring from football, Esiason has worked as a football analyst for [[CBS Sports]] on ''[[The NFL Today]]'' and [[Showtime (TV network)|Showtime]]'s ''[[Inside the NFL]]'' and was previously with [[ABC Sports|ABC]], [[HBO]], and [[NFL on Westwood One Sports|Westwood One]]. He also hosts the morning [[sports radio]] program ''[[Boomer and Gio]]'' on [[WFAN (AM)|WFAN]] in New York. 

==Early life==
Esiason was born and raised in [[East Islip, New York]].<ref>[http://repbuzz.com/story.php?id=149 RepBuzz.com<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071109165929/http://repbuzz.com/story.php?id=149 |date=November 9, 2007 }}</ref> He got the "Boomer" nickname before he was born. His mother Irene, reacting to his constant kicking in the womb, called him "Boomer," and he has kept the name since.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fabrikant |first=Geraldine |date=April 26, 1998 |title=Talking Money with Boomer Esiason; Quarterback Lets Adviser Call the Plays |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/04/26/business/talking-money-with-boomer-esiason-quarterback-lets-adviser-call-the-plays.html |access-date=September 13, 2009}}</ref>   Irene, a singer, dancer and piano player, died at the age of 37, of ovarian cancer when he was six years old. His father Norman, a veteran of WWII, never remarried, and in spite of a three-hour daily commute to New York City raised Esiason and his two sisters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eddy |first=Art |title=Boomer Esiason – My Life of Dad |url=https://www.lifeofdad.com/boomer-esiason-my-life-of-dad/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911152338/https://www.lifeofdad.com/boomer-esiason-my-life-of-dad/ |archive-date=September 11, 2018 |access-date=September 11, 2018 |website=Life of Dad }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=J. Freeman & Associates |title=Boomer Esiason's real LIFE story- a life lesson learned early |url=http://www.j-freeman.com/boomer-esiasons-reallifestory-a-life-lesson-learned-early/ |access-date=September 11, 2018 |website=J. Freeman & Associates }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Maurer |first=Tim |title=Boomer Esiason: NFL Great Turned Life Insurance Advocate |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/timmaurer/2013/09/12/boomer-esiason-nfl-great-turned-life-insurance-advocate/#2ff88a3324c1 |access-date=September 11, 2018 |website=Forbes}}</ref>  

He attended Timber Point Elementary and [[East Islip High School]], where he graduated in 1979. In high school, he was a three-sport varsity player in football, basketball, and baseball.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Smith |first=Gary |date=October 4, 1993 |title=We're Going To Beat This Thing |magazine=Sports Illustrated |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1138646/1/index.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102063506/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1138646/1/index.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 2, 2012 |access-date=June 13, 2010}}</ref>

==College career==
Esiason played college football at the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] for head coaches [[Jerry Claiborne]] and [[Bobby Ross]] and offensive coordinator [[Ralph Friedgen]]. Maryland was the only college to offer him a scholarship.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sargent |first=Dave |title=Lessons from Athletics: Boomer Esiason |url=http://www.maxpreps.com/news/p0TYIIRF2kGCmqF4d4fbvw/lessons-from-athletics--boomer-esiason.htm |access-date=September 11, 2018 |website=Max Preps |publisher=CBS Interactive}}</ref> At Maryland, he set 17 school records. He completed 461 of 850 passes (54.2 percent) for 6,169 yards and 42 touchdowns with 27 interceptions.  He was a two-time honorable mention All-American in 1982 and 1983.  In his final home game, he threw two third-quarter touchdown passes to lead a comeback victory over No. 3 [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina]] and seal the ACC title. At Maryland, his backup and roommate was future NFL quarterback and head coach [[Frank Reich]]. Boomer graduated in December 1983 with a B.A. in Communications, and received the Distinguished Alumnus Award in 1999.<ref>{{cite web |title=Esiason passes UM graduates a message; Tolerance ex-QB's focus in commencement speech |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1999/12/24/esiason-passes-um-graduates-a-message-tolerance-ex-qbs-focus-in-commencement-speech/ |website=[[Baltimore Sun]] |access-date=6 June 2024 |date=24 December 1999}}</ref>

==Professional football career==
===Cincinnati Bengals (first stint)===
Esiason was selected by the Cincinnati Bengals in the second round of the [[1984 NFL draft]] with the 38th overall pick, surprisingly low considering his successful college career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=October 10, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> [[ESPN]] draft analyst [[Mel Kiper Jr.]] was, in Esiason's words, "going ballistic" that he was still available in the latter stages of the first round. No quarterbacks were drafted in the first round; Esiason was actually the first quarterback selected. ([[Steve Young]] had signed with the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|L.A. Express]] of the now-defunct [[United States Football League]].)  Esiason's USFL territorial rights were controlled by the [[Washington Federals]], the worst team in the league.

Esiason's teammate from Maryland, [[defensive end]] [[Pete Koch]], was taken by the Bengals with the 16th pick in the first round of the same draft. Koch lasted just one season in Cincinnati and five total in the NFL.

At 6'-5" and 224 pounds, and with a powerful arm, Esiason was the signal caller on one of the most potent offenses of the late 1980s.

Boomer got his first pro start on October 7, [[1984 NFL season|1984]], in a home game against the [[1984 Houston Oilers season|Houston Oilers]]. On a rainy day, he led the Bengals to a 13–3 win over Houston, and scored the game's only touchdown on a three-yard run. He took over for [[Ken Anderson (quarterback)|Ken Anderson]] as the Bengals' full-time starting quarterback on September 22, [[1985 NFL season|1985]], in a 44–41 home loss to the [[1985 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]] and future Hall of Famer [[Dan Fouts]]. Although well short of Anderson's rushing total of over 2,200 yards, Esiason was surprisingly mobile, rushing for 1,598 yards on 447 attempts and scoring seven touchdowns by this point in his career. He became particularly adept at running the difficult "no huddle" offense devised by Bengals head coach [[Sam Wyche]].

On December 21, 1986, the final game of the [[1986 NFL season|1986 season]], Esiason set a team record by throwing five touchdown passes, as the [[1986 Cincinnati Bengals season|Bengals]] defeated the [[1986 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] 52–21. He also set the team single season passing record of 3,959 yards in this game.<ref name="rauzulusstreet.com">{{Cite web |title=nal Football League (NFL) – Cincinnati Bengals Team Records The National Football League (NFL) – Cincinnati Bengals Team Records |url=http://www.rauzulusstreet.com/football/profootball/cinncinatirecords.html |access-date=September 23, 2018 |website=Rauzulu's Street }}</ref> It was the last game of Bengals' quarterback Ken Anderson's playing career.

After leading Cincinnati to six straight wins to begin the [[1988 NFL season|1988 season]], Esiason set a dismal single game team record on October 16 by throwing 5 interceptions in a 27–21 loss to the [[1988 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]]. The team finished the season 12–4, utilizing the highest scoring offense in the NFL, and securing the organization's fifth [[AFC Central]] division title. Esiason finished the season as the NFL's top rated passer. However, he had sprained his left ankle and the index finger on his throwing hand in the last regular-season game of the season.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1989/01/30/joe-cool-the-49ers-joe-montana-knocked-the-bengals-cold-with-a-spectacular-late-rally-in-the-super-bowl | title=Super Bowl XXIII: Joe Montana, 49ers knock Bengals cold | work=Sports Illustrated Vault | SI.com }}</ref> In the playoffs, Cincinnati, bolstered by rushing, defeated first the [[1988 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] and then the [[1988 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]] to reach [[Super Bowl XXIII]], the franchise's second appearance in a [[Super Bowl]] (after [[Super Bowl XVI]]), as they faced off with the team they had lost to the first time around, the [[1988 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]].

The Super Bowl was a tight affair that saw a 3–3 halftime score, the first halftime tie in Super Bowl history. Still marred by a sore arm, Esiason threw for 144 yards on 11-of-25 passing with an interception.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nydailynews.com/1999/09/03/amp-lights-way-for-spartans/ | title=Super Bowl XXIII: Joe Montana leads 49ers to incredible comeback win over Boomer Esiason's Bengals | website=[[New York Daily News]] | date=January 9, 2014 }}</ref> Cincinnati had their points come on a kickoff return by [[Stanford Jennings]] and three field goals by [[Jim Breech]]. Bengals cornerback [[Lewis Billups]] dropped what seemed like a sure interception in the end zone when they were up 13–6 on a drive that led to a San Francisco touchdown. Despite this, they led 16–13 with three minutes remaining and San Francisco deep in their own territory. The 49ers, led by future Hall of Fame quarterback [[Joe Montana]], marched 92 yards on their last drive, scoring on a touchdown pass to receiver [[John Taylor (American football)|John Taylor]] with 34 seconds remaining in the game. A last-ditch pass by Esiason to wide receiver [[Cris Collinsworth]] was broken up, resulting in a 20–16 loss for the Bengals.

On October 29, [[1989 NFL season|1989]], Esiason tied his own record for touchdown passes in a game with five, as the Bengals demolished the [[1989 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] 56–23.<ref name="rauzulusstreet.com"/><ref>{{Cite news |title=ESIASON'S TOUCHDOWN PASSES WAKE UP BENGALS, 56–23 |language=en-US |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1989/10/30/esiasons-touchdown-passes-wake-up-bengals-56-23/132f7581-45de-4486-928b-55a325f4e5db/ |access-date=October 27, 2023 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> In that same game, the Bengals tied a team record with eight touchdowns.

On October 7, [[1990 NFL season|1990]], he threw for 490 yards (a single game team passing record) in a 34–31 victory over the [[1990 Los Angeles Rams season|Los Angeles Rams]].<ref name="rauzulusstreet.com"/>

===New York Jets===
Before the 1993 season, Esiason was traded to his hometown team, the New York Jets, in exchange for a third round pick that year (which became linebacker [[Steve Tovar]]) as well as a conditional second round pick the following year (which did not kick in).<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Eskenazi |first=Gerald |date=March 18, 1993 |title=PRO FOOTBALL; Jets Make a Left Turn With Deal for Esiason |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/03/18/sports/pro-football-jets-make-a-left-turn-with-deal-for-esiason.html |access-date=October 27, 2023 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The trade reunited Esiason with [[Bruce Coslet]], Esiason's mentor as offensive coordinator in Cincinnati, who had been hired by the Jets' to be their head coach after the Bengals 1988 Super Bowl run.<ref name=":0" /> Esiason played three seasons for the Jets, each year under a different head coach: Coslet (1993), [[Pete Carroll]] (1994), and [[Rich Kotite]] (1995). During his 1995 season with the [[1995 New York Jets season|team]], Esiason was seriously injured in a game on October 8 against the [[1995 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]] when rookie [[Everett McIver]] was whistled for a false start, and [[Bruce Smith (defensive end)|Bruce Smith]] of the Bills raced around him and caught Esiason under his face mask. Smith was terribly upset about Esiason's injury, saying that he hadn't heard a whistle blowing the play dead, and Esiason blamed the officials for not whistling until after Smith made contact. That horrific collision gave Esiason a severe concussion, his first as a player.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oct. 8 concussion continues to slow Jets' Esiason |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1995/10/19/oct-8-concussion-continues-to-slow-jets-esiason/ |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=Tampa Bay Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1995/10/13/esiason-injury-is-officials-fault/ | title=Esiason: Injury is Official's Fault | website=[[Chicago Tribune]] | date=October 13, 1995 }}</ref> When he returned to the field over a month later, it was coincidentally against the Bills.

Esiason was released by the Jets after the 1995 season.

===Arizona Cardinals===
Esiason signed with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] as a free agent in 1996. It was during this season, on November 10, [[1996 NFL season|1996]], that he threw for the fifth best passing yardage day in NFL history, with 522 yards in a 37–34 overtime victory over the [[1996 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL Passing Yards Single Game Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/pass_yds_single_game.htm |access-date=2025-01-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Two weeks later he led a fourth-quarter comeback against the playoff-bound [[1996 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]].

===Cincinnati Bengals (second stint)===
Esiason contemplated retirement in the offseason, but was talked into playing one more season with the Bengals, now with Coslet as coach. He was effective after replacing [[Jeff Blake]] midway through the 1997 campaign, throwing for 13 touchdowns against only two interceptions, and garnering a passer rating of 106.9 for the season. The Bengals were 3–8 with Blake under center. With Esiason at quarterback, they won four of their last five games and scored over 30 points four times. Twice they broke 40 points, in a 44–42 loss to the [[1997 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] and in a 41–14 win over the [[1997 Tennessee Oilers season|Tennessee Oilers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1997 Cincinnati Bengals Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/cin/1997.htm |access-date=2025-01-08 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Esiason debated closely for playing in 1998, since he liked playing for Coslet and quarterbacks coach [[Ken Anderson (quarterback)|Ken Anderson]], stating that a contract offer good enough for him to not refuse would've turned the table for him to return, as he was offered an analyst's position on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]]'s ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' for the third year in a row.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cincyjungle.com/2016/7/18/12212654/boomer-esiason-was-really-was-close-to-coming-back-to-bengals-in-1998 | title=Boomer Esiason was 'really was close to coming back' to Bengals in 1998 | date=July 18, 2016 }}</ref>

On December 21, 1997, Esiason played his last NFL game. He threw two touchdowns on the day, with a 79-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver [[Darnay Scott]] being his last touchdown pass in a 16–14 victory over the [[1997 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/E/EsiaBo00/gamelog/1997/ | title=Boomer Esiason 1997 Game Log | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199712210cin.htm | title=Baltimore Ravens at Cincinnati Bengals – December 21st, 1997 | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref>

==Records and honors==
Esiason was named to four [[Pro Bowl]] games (1986, 1988, 1989, 1993) and holds several NFL career records for left-handed quarterbacks, including most touchdown passes (247), passing yards (37,920), and completions (2,969).  He also led the AFC in passing in both 1988 and 1989.

Among the awards he has earned during his career include the [[National Football League Most Valuable Player Award|NFL Most Valuable Player Award]] in 1988 (leading the league with a [[passer rating]] of 97.4), and the [[Walter Payton Man of the Year Award]] in 1995 for his charitable work. At his retirement in 1997 he finished in the top 10 all-time in many QB career statistical categories.

Football Nation ranks him as the 25th greatest quarterback of the post-merger era.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Top 100 QBS Since the Merger (40–21) |url=http://www.footballnation.com/content/top-100-qbs-since-the-merger-40-21/15546/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121030200111/http://www.footballnation.com/content/top-100-qbs-since-the-merger-40-21/15546/ |archive-date=October 30, 2012 |access-date=October 13, 2012}}</ref>

Esiason was inducted into the [[Suffolk Sports Hall of Fame]] in the Football Category with the Class of 1990. In 2004, he was inducted into the Nassau County Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Jim |date=July 24, 2009 |title=Ridgewood 9-Year-Old's Study of Boomer Esiason Leads to WFAN Meeting |work=Ridgewood News |url=http://www.northjersey.com/arts_entertainment/radio/Ridgewood_9-year-olds__study_of_Boomer_Esiason_leads_to_WFAN_meeting.html |access-date=September 15, 2009}}</ref>

In 2023, the Bengals inducted Esiason into their Ring of Honor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bengals Ring of Honor Inducts Chad Johnson, Boomer Esiason |url=https://www.bengals.com/news/boomer-esiason-chad-johnson-ochocinco-ring-of-honor-2023 |website=Bengals.com}}</ref>

==Entertainment career==

===Television, film and literature===
Esiason has appeared in over 25 commercials including ones for Diet Coke, Wheaties, Reebok, Samsung, Hanes, Doritos and Domino's Pizza. He has also appeared in many TV shows and movies, such as ''[[The Game Plan (film)|The Game Plan]]'', ''[[Miss America 1999]]'', ''[[Spin City]]'', and ''[[Blue Bloods (TV series)|Blue Bloods]]'' among others.

He made two appearances on the game show ''[[Family Feud]]''. On March 18, 1989, he appeared in the episode "Bengals v. 49ers", reminiscent of their latest Super Bowl match.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Video: Family Feud – Bengals v. 49ers | date=February 2017 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v3S62dFmxvk | archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211110/v3S62dFmxvk| archive-date=November 10, 2021 | url-status=live|access-date=February 1, 2017 |publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> In 1993, his second Family Feud appearance came in the episode "NFC v. AFC".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Video: Family Feud – NFC v. AFC | date=February 8, 2016 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xUKgZkKOiWc | archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211110/xUKgZkKOiWc| archive-date=November 10, 2021 | url-status=live|access-date=February 8, 2016 |publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

He authored a children's reader in 1995 titled ''A Boy Named Boomer''<ref>{{Cite web |year=1995 |title=A Boy Named Boomer |url=https://archive.org/details/boynamedboomer00esia |access-date=September 19, 2018 |website=Internet Archive}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=BOOMER'S STILL BATTLING CYSTIC FIBROSIS |url=https://www.esiason.org/cf-news/boomers-still-battling-cystic-fibrosis |access-date=September 19, 2018 |website=Boomer Esiason Foundation }}</ref> and co-wrote (with Lowell Cauffiel) a 1998 novel titled ''Toss''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Toss |url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/978-0-525-94429-4 |access-date=September 19, 2018 |website=PW |publisher=PWxyz, LLC}}</ref>

===Broadcasting===
While still playing, Esiason appeared as a color analyst on the [[USA Network]]'s two-year broadcast of the [[NFL Europe#WLAF/World League (1991–92)|World League of American Football]] (WLAF) on Monday nights, partnered with [[Brad Nessler]]. After his retirement from playing, he went into broadcasting full-time. He was a [[color commentator]] for [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]]'s ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' from [[1998 NFL season|1998]] to [[1999 NFL season|1999]]. Following his dismissal by ABC in 2000, due primarily to personal conflicts between him and play-by-play announcer [[Al Michaels]],<ref>{{Cite news |date=2000-03-10 |title=TV SPORTS; Esiason Fires Back After Being Dismissed |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/03/10/sports/tv-sports-esiason-fires-back-after-being-dismissed.html |access-date=2025-08-31 |language=en}}</ref> he was hired by the Westwood One radio network to become the lead analyst for radio broadcasts of ''Monday Night Football''  and Super Bowl games. He broadcast every Super Bowl from [[Super Bowl XXXIV|2000]] to [[Super Bowl LII|2018]].<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Boomer Esiason Done With Monday Night Westwood One NFL Radio Broadcasts |url=https://www.si.com/media/2018/07/17/boomer-esiason-westwood-one-monday-night-football-broadcasts |access-date=August 31, 2025 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |date=July 17, 2018}}</ref>

As planned, after broadcasting the ''[[Thursday Night Football]]'' game on September 6, 2018, he left Westwood One.  He was quoted as saying "I’m going to miss it, but in all reality I kind of have to get part of my life back."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Best |first=Neil |title=Boomer Esiason won't return as 'Monday Night Football' radio analyst |url=https://www.newsday.com/sports/media/boomer-esiason-monday-night-football-q66509 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180717150616/https://www.newsday.com/sports/media/boomer-esiason-monday-night-football-1.19857698 |url-status=live |archive-date=July 17, 2018 |access-date=September 10, 2018 |website=Newsday }}</ref> He currently serves as an in-studio analyst ''[[Inside the NFL]]'' on Showtime, and hosts ''[[Boomer and Gio]]'' on [[WFAN (AM)|WFAN]] Radio in New York and the [[CBS Sports Network]]. In September 2012, CBS Radio announced he was added to their collection of talent to deliver five sports updates per day Monday through Friday. Esiason was also an analyst for ''[[The NFL Today]]'' on [[NFL on CBS|CBS]] television from 2002 through 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Contes |first=Brandon |title=Boomer Esiason leaving 'The NFL Today' on CBS, extends WFAN contract |url=https://awfulannouncing.com/cbs/boomer-esiason-leaving-nfl-today-extends-wfan-contract.html |website=Awful Announcing|date=April 29, 2024 }}</ref>

Starting in 2013, he began appearing once a week as a guest on ''[[The Jim Rome Show]]'' during the NFL season to break down the upcoming weekend's NFL action.

In February 2026, while on his WFAN Radio show, Esiason commented on statements by some United States Olympic athletes about representing their country, saying that American Olympians “should just pipe down and just do their sport and play for our country and respect the flag and respect everything that’s going on.”<ref name="Fox">{{cite news |last=Gaydos |first=Ryan |title=Ex-NFL star encourages American Olympians to ‘pipe down’ and ‘respect the flag’ |work=Fox News |date=February 10, 2026 |url=https://www.foxnews.com/sports/ex-nfl-star-encourages-american-olympians-pipe-down-respect-flag }}</ref> The remarks drew commentary from media figures including former ESPN producer Mike Ryan, who on ''The Dan Le Batard Show'' criticized Esiason’s position and defended the athletes’ public statements about political and social issues in the United States, stating, “They [Olympic athletes] are using their one moment, in most cases, to highlight that, because that is universally American.”<ref name="Yahoo">{{cite news |title=Boomer Esiason Ripped By Former ESPN Producer For Olympic Comments |work=Yahoo Sports |date=February 12, 2026 |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/boomer-esiason-ripped-former-espn-204655502.html }}</ref>


===WFAN morning show===
{{Main|Boomer and Gio}}
[[File:Boomer and Carton (29872193013).jpg|thumb|right|Esiason (left) with former co-host [[Craig Carton]] (right) in 2016]]
In April 2007, after the firing of [[Don Imus]], CBS Radio gave Esiason a one-week "try-out" as Imus' replacement on WFAN. The station announced him as the permanent host on August 13, with radio veteran [[Craig Carton]] joining as co-host. ''Boomer and Carton'' officially started on September 4, 2007.<ref>[http://www.wfan.com WFAN – The Fan – Sports Radio 66 Homepage<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>{{Citation needed|date=June 2008}} As an analyst with Westwood One, Esiason would do the Monday morning show, travel to do the ''Monday Night Football'' game and travel back to New York in time to do the Tuesday morning show. The ''Boomer and Carton'' radio program became the number-one rated morning show in all key demographics in the greater New York listening area and was seen on the MSG Network from 2010 to 2013. On March 8, 2013, both Esiason and Carton worked the radio broadcast of a [[Brooklyn Nets]] basketball game.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Diamond Joe |date=March 9, 2013 |title=Net Worth: Boomer And Carton Shine Working Brooklyn Nets Radio Broadcast On WFAN |url=http://sportsrants.com/media/2013/03/09/net-worth-boomer-and-carton-shine-working-brooklyn-nets-radio-broadcast-on-wfan/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104142452/http://sportsrants.com/media/2013/03/09/net-worth-boomer-and-carton-shine-working-brooklyn-nets-radio-broadcast-on-wfan/ |archive-date=November 4, 2016 |access-date=November 4, 2016 |publisher=SportsRants.com}}</ref> The radio program had been simulcast on the [[CBS Sports Network]] since January 2014.<ref name="bobsblitz-boomerandcarton">{{Cite web |title=Boomer & Carton 'Joining' CBS Sports Network in Simulcast Form |url=http://www.bobsblitz.com/2013/12/boomer-carton-joining-cbs-sports.html |access-date=December 2, 2013 |publisher=BobsBlitz.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=WFAN Morning Show TV Simulcasts To Continue. |url=http://www.insideradio.com/free/wfan-morning-show-tv-simulcasts-to-continue/article_1d7dfa3c-d54c-11e7-a70f-e3405e84ed97.html |access-date=September 10, 2018 |website=Inside Radio |date=November 29, 2017 |publisher=Insideradio.com}}</ref>

Craig Carton was arrested in September 2017 and charged with operating a concert ticket [[Ponzi scheme]]. Carton then resigned from WFAN, leaving Esiason as the sole host of the show, which was rebranded ''The Morning Show with Boomer''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kratch |first=James |date=September 14, 2017 |title=Boomer Esiason reacts to Craig Carton's WFAN exit: 'It's a sad day' |url=http://www.nj.com/sports/index.ssf/2017/09/boomer_esiason_reacts_to_craig_cartons_wfan_exit_i.html |access-date=September 14, 2017 |website=[[NJ.com]] |publisher=[[Advance Digital]]}}</ref> Gregg Giannotti joined Boomer as permanent co-host starting on January 2, 2018, with the show rechristened as ''[[Boomer and Gio]]''.

==Personal life==
In 1986, Esiason married his wife, Cheryl. They have two children, son Gunnar and daughter Sydney.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 9, 2014 |title=Boomer Esiason's Wife Cheryl Esiason |url=http://playerwags.com/boomer-esiasons-wife-cheryl-esiason/ |access-date=March 15, 2018 |website=playerwags.com}}</ref> Sydney is married to former professional hockey player [[Matt Martin (ice hockey, born 1989)|Matt Martin]].<ref name="Martin">{{Cite news |last=Longley |first=Rob |date=January 12, 2017 |title=Football great Boomer Esiason a super fan of hockey, Maple Leafs' Martin |newspaper=Toronto Sun |url=http://torontosun.com/2017/01/12/football-great-boomer-esiason-a-super-fan-of-hockey-maple-leafs-martin/wcm/e175640c-d813-4d54-9151-df77d60360fa |access-date=December 5, 2017}}</ref>

Esiason and his family have lived in the village of [[Plandome, New York]], since at least 1998.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fabrikant |first=Geraldine |date=April 26, 1998 |title=TALKING MONEY WITH: BOOMER ESIASON; Quarterback Lets Adviser Call the Plays |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/04/26/business/talking-money-with-boomer-esiason-quarterback-lets-adviser-call-the-plays.html |access-date=September 19, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Best |first=Neil |title=A trip to Mike FrancesaLand |url=https://www.newsday.com/sports/media/a-trip-to-mike-francesaland-m56562 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140319035325/http://www.newsday.com/sports/media/a-trip-to-mike-francesaland-1.7404217 |url-status=live |archive-date=March 19, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2018 |website=Newsday }}</ref>

Esiason is an avid [[ice hockey]] fan, and a devoted supporter of the [[New York Rangers]]. He is also a fan of the [[New York Mets]] and [[New York Knicks]]. As of 2019, he plays in up to 70 recreational-league hockey games a year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lane |first=Jon |date=March 19, 2019 |title=Five Questions with Boomer Esiason |url=https://www.nhl.com/news/five-questions-with-boomer-esiason/c-305905316 |access-date=June 15, 2019 |website=NHL.com |publisher=National Hockey League}}</ref> Gunnar and his father are teammates on their local hockey team. Esiason plays in the annual Mikey Strong Charity Hockey game with [[National Hockey League|NHL]] alumni.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McLoughlin |first=Caela |title=Reasons To Attend the 2019 Mikey Strong Charity Hockey Game |url=https://www.nhl.com/devils/news/reasons-to-attend-the-2019-mikey-strong-charity-hockey-game/c-305923336 |access-date=June 15, 2019 |website=NowWeRise |date=March 19, 2019 |publisher=New Jersey Devils}}</ref> His foundation sponsors the annual Guinness Cup Hockey Tournament.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2019 GUINNESS CUP HOCKEY TOURNAMENT |url=https://www.esiason.org/get-involved/event/2019-guinness-cup-hockey-tournament |access-date=June 15, 2019 |website=Boomer Esiason Foundation }}</ref>

==Boomer Esiason Foundation==
The Boomer Esiason Foundation (BEF) was formed soon after Esiason's son, Gunnar, was diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis in 1993. The Foundation was built to fund research to find a cure for cystic fibrosis. It also provides scholarships, transplant grants, hospital grants, and education and awareness of CF to help provide a higher quality of life for people with CF. The foundation has raised in excess of $100 million,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Boomer Esiason |url=https://www.esiason.org/about-us/the-team/boomer-esiason1 |access-date=May 27, 2019 |website=Boomer Esiason Foundation }}</ref> and has supported numerous hospitals, including Cincinnati Children's Hospital with the Gunnar H Esiason CF/Lung Center and Columbia Presbyterian in NYC with the Gunnar H Esiason Adult CF and Lung Program. In 2018, the foundation awarded over $400,000 in scholarships to almost 100 students.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Esiason |first=Gunnar |date=May 2019 |title=Gunnar Esiason |url=http://www.gunnaresiason.com/were-expanding-bef-scholarship-eligibility-criteria/ |website=Gunnar Esiason}}</ref> The foundation is located in New York City and runs numerous events around the country.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Boomer Esiason Foundation |url=http://www.esiason.org |access-date=May 9, 2017 |website=The Boomer Esiason Foundation}}</ref> The foundation annually receives four stars from [[Charity Navigator]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Boomer Esiason Foundation |url=https://www.charitynavigator.org/index.cfm?bay=search.summary&orgid=8199 |access-date=May 27, 2019 |website=Charity Navigator }}</ref>

In 1996, Esiason formed a partnership with [[Cantor Fitzgerald]] and [[Howard Lutnick]] (CEO) as the foundation offices were moved to the [[1 World Trade Center (1971–2001)|North Tower]] of the [[World Trade Center (1973–2001)|World Trade Center]] in lower Manhattan on the 101st floor, which was destroyed in 2001 in the [[September 11 attacks]]. All five full-time employees survived, as none were in the building at the time, but "Esiason figured he knew over 100 people personally" who were killed in the attack, including his best friend Tim O'Brien, who was a partner at Cantor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Daugherty |first=Paul |date=September 21, 2001 |title=Esiason mourns lost friend |url=http://cincinnati.com/terror/esiason21.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114165149/http://cincinnati.com/terror/esiason21.html |archive-date=January 14, 2012 |access-date=September 13, 2011 |website=The Cincinnati Enquirer}}</ref>

'''Anthony Darelle''' "'''Booger'''" '''McFarland''' (born December 18, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] at [[LSU Tigers football|Louisiana State University]] and was drafted by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the first round of the [[1999 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McFaAn20.htm |title=Anthony McFarland NFL Football Statistics |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |publisher=Sports Reference LLC |access-date=April 22, 2016}}</ref> McFarland also played for the [[Indianapolis Colts]], and won two [[Super Bowl ring]]s in his career: one with the Buccaneers ([[Super Bowl XXXVII]]) and another with the Colts ([[Super Bowl XLI]]). He was an analyst for ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' in 2018 and 2019, before joining as a pregame analyst on ''[[Monday Night Countdown]]'' in 2020.

==Early life==
{{Expand section|date=December 2023}}
McFarland and his two siblings grew up in [[Winnsboro, Louisiana]].<ref name="v775">{{cite web | last=Stroud | first=Rick | title=Triumph from tragedy | website=Tampa Bay Times | date=2005-11-27 | url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/2005/11/27/triumph-from-tragedy/ | access-date=2024-12-27}}</ref> He attended Winnsboro High School, where he was an All-State lineman for the Wildcats.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Allen |first=Teddy |date=February 9, 2019 |title=Still Booger, but not a booger anymore |url=https://www.thenewsstar.com/story/news/local/blogs/2019/02/09/still-booger-but-not-booger-anymore/2812021002/ |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=The News-Star |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Joey |date=2015-01-23 |title=McFarland credits early discipline to continued success |url=https://www.hannapub.com/franklinsun/mcfarland-credits-early-discipline-to-continued-success/article_e9e69860-a31b-11e4-8dc1-0ff4e26a9a1e.html |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=Hanna Newspapers |language=en}}</ref>

McFarland received the nickname "[[Mucus|Booger]]" as a child, saying "I was a bad kid, getting into a lot of wild stuff. I used to get called a lot of different things. But that was just the one that stuck."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20040917/hawk17/moore-and-mcfarland-battle-of-the-boogers |title=Moore and McFarland: Battle of the Boogers |last=Bishop, Greg |date=September 17, 2004 |access-date=October 21, 2019 |website=SeattleTimes.com}}</ref>

== College career ==
McFarland played for the LSU Tigers football team from 1995 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://lsusports.net/sports/fb/roster/player/anthony-mcfarland/ |title=Anthony McFarland Bio |website=LSUsports.net |date=July 3, 2019 |access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> In his freshman year, he started every game at defensive tackle, finishing the season with 73 tackles (including 12 tackles for loss and 2 quarterback sacks) and quickly became a crowd favorite for pulling double-duty at the fullback position for short-yardage plays.  He also recorded a tackle in LSU's victory over Michigan State at the [[1995 Independence Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://static.lsusports.net/custompages/assets/docs/fb/pdf/19951229.pdf |title=Louisiana State Tigers vs Michigan State Spartans, 12/29/95: Final Defensive Statistics |date=December 29, 1995 |website=LSUSports.net |page=4 |access-date=October 7, 2019}}</ref> For the rest of his collegiate career from his sophomore year onward, he focused on defensive tackle, and helped bring the Tigers to two further bowl wins in the [[1996 Peach Bowl]] and the [[1997 Independence Bowl]], also earning 1996 Peach Bowl SEC Defensive MVP honors. Despite a spectacular collapse by the Tigers in the 1998 season, McFarland was named defensive co-captain his senior year, earned first-team All-SEC and All-America honors, and played in the 1999 [[Senior Bowl]]. He graduated in 1999 with a degree in business management.

McFarland was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the first round with the 15th overall pick in the [[1999 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In eight seasons with the team, he totaled 305 tackles and 20 sacks over 84 games, and won [[Super Bowl XXXVII]] in 2002.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2629943 |title=Colts acquire Bucs' McFarland for second-round pick |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |date=October 17, 2006 |website=ESPN.com |access-date=January 26, 2019 |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

On October 17, 2006, McFarland was traded to the [[Indianapolis Colts]] for a second-round pick in the [[2007 NFL draft]].<ref name="y767">{{cite web | title=Bucs trade DT Booger McFarland to Colts | website=WTSP.com | date=2006-10-17 | url=https://www.wtsp.com/article/sports/bucs-trade-dt-booger-mcfarland-to-colts/67-396119883 | access-date=2024-12-27}}</ref> The trade reunited him with [[Tony Dungy]], his head coach in Tampa Bay during his first three seasons. At the time of the trade, the Colts ranked last in the league in run defense, allowing over 116 yards per-game, and had lost defensive tackle [[Corey Simon]] to a season-ending injury the week before. McFarland made his first sack as a member of the Colts against the [[Buffalo Bills]] on November 10. He finished the regular season with 33 tackles and 2.5 sacks, although the Colts finished last in rush defense.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony McFarland 2006 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McFaAn20/gamelog/2006/ |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In the playoffs, the Colts defense became stifling, limiting the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] to 44 rushing yards, the [[Baltimore Ravens]] to 83 and the [[New England Patriots]] to 93. McFarland started in [[Super Bowl XLI]] and recorded a sack, as the Colts defeated the [[Chicago Bears]], 29–17, capturing his second Super Bowl ring.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XLI - Indianapolis Colts vs. Chicago Bears - February 4th, 2007 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200702040chi.htm |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

He suffered a career-ending knee injury the following training camp.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.indystar.com/story/sports/nfl/colts/2018/08/20/remembering-former-colts-player-booger-mcfarland-who-announced-game-monday-night-football/1047546002/ |title=Remembering former Colts player Booger McFarland, who announced game on 'Monday Night Football' |last=Horner |first=Scott |date=August 20, 2018 |website=Indianapolis Star |access-date=January 26, 2019}}</ref>

== Broadcasting career ==

[[File:Booger McFarland - 2018 SEC Summerfest (cropped).jpg|thumb|left|McFarland in 2018]]

McFarland co-hosted a radio show with [[Marc Ryan (radio personality)|Marc Ryan]] on Tampa [[sports radio]] station [[WKVZ|WHFS]] until an ownership change in December 2014 resulted in the station's entire airstaff being released for a music format.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.allaccess.com/net-news/archive/story/136187/98-7-the-fan-tampa-drops-sports-stunting-until-new |title=98.7 The Fan/Tampa Drops Sports, Stunting Until New Format Debut January 5th |date=December 4, 2014 |publisher=All Access Music Group |access-date=January 9, 2017}}</ref> He joined the [[SEC Network]] in 2014 as a football analyst. McFarland was also a part-time guest analyst on [[ESPN]]'s ''[[Mike & Mike]]'' morning program. McFarland was a color analyst for ESPN's ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' telecasts, after arriving with [[Jason Witten]] in 2018. Prior to his promotion to color analyst, McFarland was a sideline reporter and consultant during the ''Monday Night Football'' broadcasts where he announced from atop a crane-like contraption nicknamed the "Booger Mobile."<ref name="BoogerMobileY">{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/espn-defends-obstructing-nfl-views-booger-mobile-002725772.html |title=ESPN defends obstructing NFL views with 'Booger mobile' |last=Owens |first=Jason |date=October 23, 2018 |publisher=Yahoo Sports |access-date=November 12, 2018}}</ref> After receiving criticism for blocking the view of fans seated near the field, the contraption was modified to be less obstructive.<ref name="BoogerMobile">{{Cite news |url=https://ftw.usatoday.com/2018/10/monday-night-football-booger-mcfarland-mobile-crane-obstructed-view-fans |title=Booger McFarland's crane is ruining 'Monday Night Football' for some fans |last=Curtis |first=Charles |date=October 23, 2018 |work=USA Today |access-date=November 12, 2018}}</ref><ref name="BoogerMobileMod">{{Cite web |url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2018/10/30/espn-makes-revisions-to-booger-mobile/ |title=ESPN makes revisions to Booger mobile |last=Florio |first=Mike |date=October 30, 2018 |publisher=Pro Football Talk |access-date=November 12, 2018}}</ref> McFarland was promoted to color analyst in May 2019 after Witten left to return to the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/espn-not-adding-anyone-to-monday-night-football-booth-booger-mc-farland-gets-big-chance-144209165.html |title=ESPN not adding anyone to 'Monday Night Football' booth, Booger McFarland gets big chance |last=Schwab |first=Frank |date=May 1, 2019 |publisher=Yahoo Sports |access-date=October 7, 2019}}</ref> In May 2020, he and play-by-play announcer [[Joe Tessitore]] were reassigned by ESPN amid criticism from viewers.<ref>{{cite web|title=What ESPN's 'Monday Night Football' booth may look like after shakeup|url=https://nypost.com/2020/05/09/espns-monday-night-football-shakeup-begins-whats-next/|author=Andrew Marchand|website=New York Post|publisher=NYP Holdings, Inc.|date=May 9, 2020}}</ref> In dubbing ''MNF'' as "the worst (show) on television," UK newspaper ''[[The Guardian]]'' called McFarland "awful as a national NFL voice. He sounds like he's started a sentence and has no idea where it's going to end."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2019/nov/26/monday-night-football-espn-booger-mcfarland-joe-tessitore-nfl|title=Monday Night Football: the once great NFL show is now the worst on television|work= The Guardian, UK|date=November 26, 2019 |last1=Connolly |first1=Oliver }}</ref>

For the 2020 season, McFarland replaced [[Tom Jackson (American football, born 1951)|Tom Jackson]] on [[NFL Primetime]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Casselberry |first1=Ian |title=Booger McFarland will co-host NFL PrimeTime with Chris Berman for 2020 season |url=https://awfulannouncing.com/espn/booger-mcfarland-will-co-host-nfl-primetime-with-chris-berman-for-2020-season.html |website=awfulannouncing.com |date=September 9, 2020 |access-date=24 September 2020}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
McFarland is married to Tammie McFarland. They have two children.<ref name="s515">{{cite web | last=Kleinpeter | first=Jim | title=Former LSU Tiger Booger McFarland tackles Tampa air waves as sports talk-show host | website=NOLA.com | date=2013-12-29 | url=https://www.nola.com/sports/former-lsu-tiger-booger-mcfarland-tackles-tampa-air-waves-as-sports-talk-show-host/article_71c13631-019e-50f8-8af1-b4ac0a509fc8.html | access-date=2024-10-30}}</ref> McFarland is a [[Christianity|Christian]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sportsspectrum.com/podcast/2019/09/06/new-podcast-booger-mcfarland-former-nfl-player-monday-night-football-analyst/ |title=NEW PODCAST: Booger McFarland – Former NFL Player, Monday Night Football Analyst |last=Romano |first=Jason |website=Sports Spectrum |date=September 6, 2019 |access-date=September 9, 2019}}</ref>

{{Short description|American football player (born 1981)}} {{Use American English|date=November 2024}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2024}} {{Infobox NFL biography | name = Boomer Grigsby | image = Boomer Grigsby.jpg | image_size = | caption = Grigsby in 2006 | number = 51, 46 | position = [[Linebacker]], [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1981|11|15}} | birth_place = [[Canton, Illinois]], U.S. | height_ft = 5 | height_in = 11 | weight_lbs = 237 | high_school = [[Canton High School (Illinois)|Canton]] | college = [[Illinois State Redbirds football|Illinois State]] | draftyear = 2005 | draftround = 5 | draftpick = 138 | pastteams = * [[Kansas City Chiefs]] ({{NFL Year|2005}}–{{NFL Year|2007}}) * [[Miami Dolphins]] ({{NFL Year|2008}}) * [[Houston Texans]] ({{NFL Year|2009}})* | highlights = * 3× [[Division I (NCAA)#Football Championship Subdivision|Division I-AA]] [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] (2002–2004) * 3× Gateway Player of the Year (2002–2004) * 3× All-[[Missouri Valley Football Conference|Gateway]] (2002–2004) | statlabel1 = [[Tackle (football move)|Total tackles]] | statvalue1 = 36 | statlabel2 = [[Reception (American football)|Receptions]] | statvalue2 = 2 | statlabel3 = [[Receiving yards]] | statvalue3 = 14 | pfr = ThorCr00 | CollegeHOF = 2488 }} '''James Harvey''' "'''Boomer'''" '''Grigsby''' (born November 15, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Illinois State Redbirds football|Illinois State Redbirds]], and was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the fifth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. Grigsby was also a member of the [[Miami Dolphins]] and [[Houston Texans]]. ==Early life== Grigsby attended and played [[high school football]] at [[Canton High School (Illinois)|Canton High School]] where he was an all-area [[linebacker]] during his senior season.{{cite web | title = TEAM: Roster Boomer Grigsby Profile | work = MiamiDolphins.com | url = http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=33142 | accessdate = 9 July 2008 | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080812224156/http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=33142 | archivedate = 12 August 2008 }} He was not recruited to play [[college football]] until an [[Illinois State University|Illinois State]] coach saw him lifting weights in his high school's weight room. ==College career== Grigsby was a four-year letterman at [[Illinois State University]]. As a sophomore, he set a school record with 179 tackles and also recorded what would remain a career-high four sacks. The following season, Grigsby tied his own school record with 179 tackles. He came in second behind only future [[Kansas City Chiefs]] teammate [[Jared Allen]] in the voting for the [[Buck Buchanan Award]], given annually to the top defensive player in [[Division I (NCAA)#Football Championship Subdivision|Division I-AA]]. In 44 games (40 starts), at Illinois State, Grigsby recorded a school record 580 tackles to go along with 41.5 tackles for a loss, 13 sacks, six fumble recoveries, five forced fumbles and seven passes defended. He was [[Missouri Valley Football Conference|Gateway Football Conference]] Player of the Year, a Division I-AA [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] and Buchanan award finalist each of his final three seasons. ==Professional career== ===Kansas City Chiefs=== Grigsby was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the fifth round (138th overall) of the [[2005 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} On July 15, he signed a three-year, $1.067 million contract with the team.{{cite web|url=http://www.kffl.com/player/12062/nfl/news |title=KFFL - Boomer Grigsby, FB |work=KFFL.com |accessdate=9 July 2008 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141204204954/http://www.kffl.com/player/12062/nfl/news |archivedate=December 4, 2014 }} It included a signing bonus of $142,000 and base salaries of $230,000 (2005), $310,000 (2006) and $385,000 (2007). Grigsby played in all 16 regular season games that year in a reserve role and finished third on the team with 19 special teams tackles. {{Quote box | quote = "Boomer Grigsby has as much presence at the position as anybody I've been around at the start of his career." | source = [[Gunther Cunningham]],
Chiefs defensive coordinator | width = 200px | align =left }} Appearing in 15 games in 2006, Grigsby again ranked third on the Chiefs in special teams tackles with 18. He missed one game that season with foot injury. Prior to the 2007 regular season, Grigsby was converted from [[linebacker]] to [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]]. The transition was chronicled on the [[HBO]] reality series ''[[Hard Knocks (documentary series)#Kansas City Chiefs (2007)|Hard Knocks:Training Camp with the Kansas City Chiefs]]''. Despite the position change and an injury to his ribs during the preseason, Grigsby made the team. He went on to appear in 13 games for the Chiefs that season including one start. His first NFL reception came on a nine-yard pass from [[quarterback]] [[Brodie Croyle]] against the [[2007 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] on December 9, and he finished the season with two receptions for 14 yards. He finished third on the team in special teams tackles (12) for the third straight season. A [[restricted free agent]] in the 2008 offseason, Grigsby was not tendered a contract by the Chiefs and became an [[unrestricted free agent]].{{cite web | title = Free Agency Wire -- 3/1/08 | work = Scout.com | url = http://sea.scout.com/2/733726.html | accessdate = 9 July 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110716021315/http://sea.scout.com/2/733726.html | archive-date = 16 July 2011 | url-status = dead }} ===Miami Dolphins=== On March 4, 2008, Grigsby agreed to terms on a one-year contract with the [[Miami Dolphins]]. The signing reunited him with current Dolphins [[running back]]s coach [[James Saxon (American football)|James Saxon]], who was Grigsby's position coach with the Chiefs in 2007. Grigsby won the team's starting fullback job in 2008 after incumbent [[Reagan Mauia]] was released during final cuts. However, after starting the Dolphins' season opener against the [[New York Jets]] on September 7, Grigsby was released by the team two days later in favor of free agent [[Casey Cramer]]. He spent the rest of the season out of football. ===Houston Texans=== Grigsby was signed by the [[Houston Texans]] on May 12, 2009. He was waived with an injury designation on August 18. After going unclaimed on waivers, he reverted to Texans' [[injured reserve]]. He was released with an injury settlement on August 25. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{College Football HoF|2488}} {{Chiefs2005DraftPicks}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Grigsby, Boomer}} [[Category:1981 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American football fullbacks]] [[Category:American football linebackers]] [[Category:Houston Texans players]] [[Category:21st-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:Illinois State Redbirds football players]] [[Category:Kansas City Chiefs players]] [[Category:Miami Dolphins players]] [[Category:College Football Hall of Fame inductees]] [[Category:People from Canton, Illinois]] [[Category:Sportspeople from Fulton County, Illinois]] [[Category:Players of American football from Illinois]]

(Jacksonville, Florida) | college = [[Bethune–Cookman Wildcats football|Bethune-Cookman]] |draftyear=1982 |draftround=2 |draftpick=32 |pastteams= * [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] ({{NFL Year|1982}}–{{NFL Year|1984}}) * [[Los Angeles Rams]] (1984–{{NFL Year|1985}}) * [[Atlanta Falcons]] ({{NFL Year|1987}}) |statlabel1=[[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] |statvalue1=2.0 |statlabel2=[[Interception]]s |statvalue2=2 |pfr=R/ReesBo20 }} '''Booker Reese''' (September 20, 1959 – March 30, 2026) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for four seasons with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1982 to 1985. Although not picked until the second round in the [[1982 NFL draft]], Reese is considered to be the biggest draft bust in Buccaneers history due to the unusual circumstances in which he was ultimately chosen.{{cite magazine|title=Say It Ain't So: Tampa Bay Buccaneers|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/news/2001/02/12/sayitaintso_buccaneers/|url-status=dead|magazine=Sports Illustrated|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20010618012451/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/news/2001/02/12/sayitaintso_buccaneers/|archivedate=June 18, 2001|access-date=March 18, 2006}} ==Biography== Reese played [[college football]] for the [[Bethune–Cookman Wildcats football|Bethune–Cookman Wildcats]] and was selected in the second round of the [[1982 NFL draft]] by the Buccaneers. The Buccaneers intended to draft him in the first round, but a broken communication resulted in their mistakenly drafting [[Sean Farrell (American football)|Sean Farrell]].{{cite web |last1=Banks |first1=Don |title=The Most Botched NFL Draft Pick Ever |url=https://www.si.com/longform/nfl-draft-82/index.html |website=Sports Illustrated Longform |language=en |access-date=2019-08-05 |archive-date=2019-11-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191104144003/https://www.si.com/longform/nfl-draft-82/index.html |url-status=dead }} Lacking a second round pick in 1982, the Buccaneers were so convinced of Reese's talent that they traded a future first round pick in the [[1983 NFL draft]] to the [[Chicago Bears]] in order to draft Reese with the 32nd pick overall. This ill-advised transaction was consummated in spite of what was by then practically common knowledge that 1983 would be a particularly strong draft class. Although highly talented, Reese had trouble making the mental adjustment to professional football. Frustration over his inability to excel, along with his unpreparedness for the NFL lifestyle, led to problems with alcohol and cocaine. Reese's best season in the NFL came in [[1983 in sports|1983]]. He played in all 16 games that season, scoring one [[quarterback sack|sack]] and two [[interception]]s. Reese only lasted two seasons with the Bucs before being traded to the Rams for a 12th round draft pick in [[1984 in sports|1984]]. He played eleven games with the Rams, who then sent him to rehab and released him. He signed with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in [[1985 in sports|1985]], but was released before the season after again failing a drug test.{{cite web|author=Gary Shelton|title=Opportunity Lost|url=http://www.sptimes.com/2003/07/27/Columns/Opportunity_Lost.shtml|accessdate=2014-05-06}} Ironically, the man that the Buccaneers drafted initially due to the communication error, [[Sean Farrell (American football)|Sean Farrell]], would go on to have a productive NFL career that lasted a decade. Reese served two two-year sentences at Okaloosa Correctional Institution for [[cocaine]] possession and parole violation: one from 2002 to 2004, and another from 2005 to 2007.{{cite web|title=Florida Department of Corrections: Inmate Release Information Detail|url=http://www.dc.state.fl.us/InmateReleases/detail.asp?Bookmark=1&From=list&SessionID=55112823|accessdate=2014-05-06}} Reese died on March 30, 2026 at the age of 66.[https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/tampabaytimes/name/booker-reese-obituary?id=61315702 Booker Reese] Legacy ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060530074503/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=REESEBOO01 DBFB Profile]}} {{Buccaneers1982DraftPicks}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Reese, Booker}} [[Category:1959 births]] [[Category:2026 deaths]] [[Category:Players of American football from Jacksonville, Florida]] [[Category:Jean Ribault High School alumni]] [[Category:American football defensive linemen]] [[Category:Tampa Bay Buccaneers players]] [[Category:Bethune–Cookman Wildcats football players]] [[Category:NFL replacement players]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:Prisoners and detainees of Florida]]

'''Bobby L. McCray Jr.''' (born August 8, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for seven seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]].  He was selected by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] in the seventh round of the [[2004 NFL draft]], and also played for the [[New Orleans Saints]] and [[Philadelphia Eagles]] of the NFL.

==Early life ==

McCray was born in [[Miami, Florida]], in 1981.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby McCray Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McCrBo20.htm |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He attended [[Homestead High School (Homestead, Florida)|Homestead High School]] in Homestead, Florida,<ref name=dbfprofile>databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110708234407/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=MCCRABOB01  Bobby McCray]}}.  Retrieved May 6, 2011.</ref> and he played for the Homestead Broncos high school football team.<ref name=ufprofile>GatorZone.com, Football History, 2003 Roster, [http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2003&bio=mccray.html  Bobby McCray] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402034543/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/bios.php?year=2003&bio=mccray.html |date=April 2, 2012 }}.  Retrieved May 6, 2011.</ref>  As a senior, McCray was named to Prep Star's All-America team despite missing half of the season with an injury.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He had thirty-two tackles with seven quarterback sacks.<ref name=ufprofile/>

== College career ==

McCray accepted an athletic scholarship to attend the [[University of Florida]] in Gainesville, Florida, where he played for coach [[Steve Spurrier]] and coach [[Ron Zook]]'s [[Florida Gators football]] teams from [[2000 Florida Gators football team|2000]] to [[2003 Florida Gators football team|2003]].<ref name=ufmediaguide>''[http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf  2011 Florida Gators Football Media Guide] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402035222/http://web.gatorzone.com/football/media/2011/media_guide.pdf |date=April 2, 2012 }}'', University Athletic Association, Gainesville, Florida, pp. 97 & 183 (2011).  Retrieved August 30, 2011.</ref>  As a true freshman in 1999, he was [[redshirted]] by the Gators coaching staff.<ref name=ufprofile/>  During the Gators' [[2000 Florida Gators football team|2000]], he played in three games.<ref name=ufprofile/>  As a redshirt sophomore in [[2001 Florida Gators football team|2001]], he saw action in eight of eleven regular season games with two starts, and registered twelve tackles and seven "big plays" (2.5 sacks, 2.5 tackles-for-loss and two forced fumbles).<ref name=ufprofile/>

During his [[2002 Florida Gators football team|2002]] season, McCray played in all thirteen games, starting in five, and was a second-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] (SEC) selection by ''[[The Sporting News]]''.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He recorded forty-five tackles (twenty solo), and 22.3 "big plays" (2.3 sacks, four tackles-for-loss, a forced fumble, a fumble recovery, and a block).<ref name=ufprofile/>  As a senior in [[2003 Florida Gators football team|2003]], he earned second-team All-SEC honors.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He played in twelve games, started in eight and finished with fifty tackles, 11.5 tackles for loss and 9.5 sacks.<ref name=ufprofile/>

In his four-season college career, McCray appeared in thirty-six games for the Gators, including fifteen starts and thirteen in the final two years.<ref name=ufprofile/>  He recorded 107 tackles with 14.5 sacks, 20.5 stops for losses, thirty-one quarterback pressures, two pass deflections, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery.<ref name=ufprofile/>

== Professional career ==

=== Jacksonville Jaguars ===

The [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] selected McCray in the seventh round of the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> He played for the Jaguars for four seasons from {{NFL Year|2004}} to {{NFL Year|2007}}.<ref name=nflprofile>National Football League, Current Players, [http://www.nfl.com/players/bobbymccray/profile?id=MCC663361  Bobby McCray].  Retrieved May 7, 2011.</ref>  As a rookie, he played in all sixteen of the Jaguars' regular season games, made seven starts and recorded 25 tackles (18 solo) and 3.5 sacks. In 2005, he played in all 16 games for the second consecutive season with one start and collected 23 tackles (20 solo) along with 5.5 sacks.  In 2006, he started 12 games and totaled 49 tackles (42 solo), 10 sacks and two forced fumbles. In 2007 McCray saw action in 14 games along the Jacksonville defensive line, making nine starts, and recorded 24 tackles, three sacks, batted down three passes and forced a fumble. He also started both postseason games and notched four tackles, a sack and a forced fumble, McCray had a sack and forced a fumble on [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]' [[quarterback]] [[Ben Roethlisberger]] that won the Jaguars the 2007 AFC wild card game.

=== New Orleans Saints ===

On March 2, 2008, McCray signed a five-year, $20 million contract with the [[New Orleans Saints]]. The contract included $5 million in guaranteed money.  In 2008, he played in 16 games, made eight starts and had six sacks.

In 2009, McCray played in 16 games as a reserve, but he started in all three of the Saints' post-season games leading to the team's win in [[Super Bowl XLIV]].  In the first playoff game, against [[Arizona Cardinals|Arizona]], after Cardinals quarterback [[Kurt Warner]] threw an interception, McCray made a hard, but legal, block that briefly put Warner out of the game; McCray's teammate [[Darren Sharper]] described McCray's play as "game-changing".<ref>James Varney, "[http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2010/01/bobby_mccrays_block_on_kurt_wa.html  Bobby McCray's block on Kurt Warner 'game-changing' for New Orleans Saints]," ''Times-Picayune'' (January 16, 2010).  Retrieved May 6, 2011.</ref>  The following week, McCray was fined $20,000 for illegal hits on [[Minnesota Vikings]] Quarterback [[Brett Favre]] in the 2010 NFC Championship game.

After a season with the New Orleans Saints McCray earned the name "Quarterback Killa."

McCray along with the rest of the New Orleans Saints visited President Obama at the White house, 2010 National Football League Super Bowl champions August 9, 2010 in Washington, DC.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.zimbio.com/photos/Bobby+McCray/9WnOyGXrTGs/NFL+Champions+New+Orleans+Saints+Visit+President|title=Bobby McCray Photostream|website=Zimbio.com|access-date=December 6, 2021}}</ref>

McCray was released on June 21, 2010.<ref>"[https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5312088  Saints release DE McCray]," ESPN.com (June 21, 2010).  Retrieved May 6, 2011.</ref>  He was re-signed to a one-year contract by the Saints on July 22, 2010.<ref>Gregg Rosenthal, "[http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2010/07/22/saints-re-sign-bobby-mccray/  Saints re-sign Bobby McCray]," NBC Sports (July 20, 2010).  Retrieved May 6, 2011.</ref>  He was waived on September 3, 2010.

McCray dedicated his 2008 season to [[After-School All-Stars|After School All-Stars]], a national organization that provides comprehensive after school programs that are fun for kids and also keep them safe and help them succeed in school and life. With every sack that Bobby accumulates, he donates $1000 to the organization.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/bobby_mccray.html |title=EAG: Entertainers and Athletes Group : Sports Management . Marketing . Publicity |access-date=August 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130711044651/http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/bobby_mccray.html |archive-date=July 11, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Featured in [[ESPN]], McCray for volunteering at the LA Parks and Recreation Department.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/news/story?id=4271419|title=Backup plan: Bobby McCray|date=June 19, 2009|website=ESPN.com|access-date=December 6, 2021}}</ref> Also, featured in ESPN The Magazine NHL Preview Issue, October 2010,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/espn_nhl/index.html |title=Bobby McCray's - ESPN the Magazine NHL Preview Issue, October 2010 |access-date=August 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923232339/http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/espn_nhl/index.html |archive-date=September 23, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Louisiana Health & Fitness magazine, September 2009 <ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/LouisianaHealthFitness_September2009/index.html |title=Archived copy |access-date=August 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923232339/http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/LouisianaHealthFitness_September2009/index.html |archive-date=September 23, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and  New Orleans Magazine<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/neworleans_html/index.html |title=Bobby McCray New Orleans Magazine |access-date=August 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923232339/http://www.eagsportsmanagement.com/newmag/bobby_mcCray/neworleans_html/index.html |archive-date=September 23, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Philadelphia Eagles ===
McCray was signed by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] on December 30, 2010.<ref>"{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20121106100115/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/09000d5d81d520ef/article/injurydepleted-eagles-sign-dlinemen-mcray-clark Injury-depleted Eagles sign D-linemen McCray, Clark]}}," NFL.com (December 30, 2010). '''Robert Lee Sippio Jr.''' (born December 4, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was signed by the [[Peoria Pirates]] in 2002. He played [[college football]] for the [[Western Kentucky Hilltoppers football|Western Kentucky Hilltoppers]]. During Sippio's professional career, he played for thirteen different teams in four different leagues, including the NFL's [[Miami Dolphins]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]], and [[Detroit Lions]].

==College career==
Sippio played [[college football]] at Western Kentucky for three seasons. He attended Osceola High School in [[Kissimmee, Florida|Kissimmee]], [[Florida]] where he played [[High school football|football]] and [[basketball]]. He played [[cornerback]] along with former NFL player [[Brett Williams (offensive lineman)|Brett Williams]].

==Professional career==

===af2===
Sippio began playing professional football in 2002 with the [[Peoria Pirates]] of [[af2]] and then the [[Greensboro Prowlers]], before signing with the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]].

===Dallas Desperados===
Sippio played in 15 games as a [[rookie]] with the [[Dallas Desperados]], recording 75 receptions for 1,217 yards and 32 touchdowns, and recording 25.0 tackles, two interceptions and three passes broken up. He made his Arena Football League debut February 8 vs. the [[Carolina Cobras]], catching four passes for 78 yards and two touchdowns. He was named co-Offensive Player of the Game March 6 against the [[Grand Rapids Rampage]] after catching 6 passes for 116 yards and three touchdowns.

Sippio played in 16 games in his second season with Dallas, recording 61 receptions for 863 yards and 22 touchdowns and added 30.5 tackles, two interceptions and nine passes broken up. He scored touchdowns in five different ways during the season, receiving, rushing, interception return, fumble return and kickoff return.

===Tampa Bay Storm===
Sippio played in nine games for the [[Tampa Bay Storm]], recording 55 receptions for 666 yards and 18 touchdowns, before being released March 28 and claimed by the [[Chicago Rush]] on March 29.

===Chicago Rush===
After signing with Chicago, Sippio changed positions from WR/DB to OS. He finished the [[2006 Chicago Rush season|2006 season]] with 93 receptions for 1,320 yards and 35 touchdowns. He recorded a season high 10 receptions for 136 yards and two touchdowns against the [[Orlando Predators]] on February 19. He also led the league with 53 touchdowns.

===Kansas City Chiefs===
After the [[2007 Arena Football League season]], Sippio signed with the Kansas City Chiefs on August 12, 2007. His signing appeared on [[HBO]]'s ''[[Hard Knocks (documentary series)|Hard Knocks]]'', a program showcasing [[National Football League Training Camp|NFL training camps]]. On September 1, 2007, the Chiefs made their final cuts to 53, and Sippio made the final roster. However, he was released on September 2 to make room for [[Tyler Thigpen]].<ref>[http://www.kansascity.com/sports/chiefs/story/258335.html http://www.kansascity.com/sports/chiefs/story/258335.html]</ref> The following day, Sippio was added to the Chiefs [[practice squad]]. He was signed to the active roster on September 11, 2007, to replace [[Eddie Kennison]] who suffered a [[hamstring]] injury.<ref>[http://www.kansascity.com/news/breaking_news/story/270713.html http://www.kansascity.com/news/breaking_news/story/270713.html]</ref>

Sippio was released by the Chiefs on August 30, 2008.

===Chicago Slaughter===
On May 13, 2009, due to the injury of leading wide receiver [[Donovan Morgan (American football)|Donovan Morgan]], the [[Chicago Slaughter]] of the [[Continental Indoor Football League]] signed Sippio.<ref name="ESPN/chicago/story?id=4165113">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/chicago/story?id=4165113|title=Slaughter sign former Rush WR Sippio|date=May 13, 2009|publisher=ESPNChicago.com|access-date=2009-05-14}}</ref> The [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]] halted operations for the 2009 season, preventing Sippio from re-signing with the Rush or any other AFL team.

===California Redwoods===
Sippio signed with the [[California Redwoods]] of the [[United Football League (2009)|United Football League]] in 2009, but was released in August so he could sign with the [[Detroit Lions]].<ref>[http://www.ufl-football.com/press/2009/08/25/ufl_s_florida_tuskers_announce_signing_of_12_additional_players_including_quarterback_craig_nall UFL's Florida Tuskers Announce Signing of 12 Additional Players Including Quarterback Craig Nall] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090828164929/http://www.ufl-football.com/press/2009/08/25/ufl_s_florida_tuskers_announce_signing_of_12_additional_players_including_quarterback_craig_nall |date=2009-08-28 }}</ref>

===Detroit Lions===
Sippio was signed by the [[Detroit Lions]] on August 7, 2009, after [[offensive lineman]] [[Damion Cook]] was placed on [[injured reserve]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.prideofdetroit.com/2009/8/7/981112/damion-cook-out-for-season-lions|title=Damion Cook Out for Season; Lions Sign Bobby Sippio|date=7 August 2009}}</ref> He was waived on August 17 when the team signed [[wide receiver]] [[Dane Looker]].

===Florida Tuskers===
Sippio was signed by the [[Florida Tuskers]] of the [[United Football League (2009)|United Football League]] on November 16, 2009. He played for then-head coach [[Jay Gruden]].

===Orlando Predators===

Sippio signed with the Predators on April 13, 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/?id=4383674|title = Predators Sign WR Bobby Sippio|date = 13 April 2012}}</ref> Sippio scored 6 TDs (4 receiving, 2 rushing), including a game-winner with just 8.7 seconds remaining, in Orlando's 73–69 victory over #1 seed Jacksonville in the first round of the 2010 Arena Football Playoffs.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://arenafootball.com/news/?article_id%3D271 |title=Archived copy |accessdate=2010-08-08 |url-status=usurped |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707161603/http://arenafootball.com/news/?article_id=271 |archivedate=2011-07-07 }}</ref>

==Legal trouble==
On May 25, 2012,  Bobby Sippio was arrested and charged with [[attempted murder]], armed [[robbery]], aggravated battery, and [[kidnapping]] over an incident involving his girlfriend's brother. Sippio and a friend allegedly arrived at the man's apartment under the pretense of helping to move furniture, but instead they forced him into a vehicle at gunpoint, drove to an unpopulated area, then proceeded to beat and threaten the man before eventually returning him home. The man, Sergio Moore, suffered a broken nose, swollen left hand and wrist, and cuts to the head and cheek.<ref>{{cite web| url = http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/2012-05-26/news/os-predators-bobby-sippio-arrest-20120525_1_bobby-sippio-orlando-predators-murder-charge| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120528094225/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/2012-05-26/news/os-predators-bobby-sippio-arrest-20120525_1_bobby-sippio-orlando-predators-murder-charge| archive-date = 2012-05-28| title = Orlando Predators Bobby Sippio: Orlando Predators arena football player Bobby Sippio arrested - Orlando Sentinel}}</ref> All charges were dropped on September 12, 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://courts.osceolaclerk.com/BenchmarkWeb/CourtCase.aspx/Details/2545727?digest=c5tNvhaRkfuTcNi0CD7u1g|title = Osceola County case 2015 CF 001889  |date = 12 September 2016}}</ref>

'''Jeffrey Boone Stutz''' (born November 4, 1982) was a former [[tight end]] and [[long snapper]] for [[Texas A&M University]] and [[long snapper]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was released by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] on December 11, 2007. Stutz is the son of Barbara and Paul Stutz of [[Arlington, Texas]].

==Early life==
He met then [[Texas Christian University|TCU]] head coach [[Dennis Franchione]] and planned to walk on for the [[TCU Horned Frogs|Horned Frogs]]. When Franchione became the head coach at [[University of Alabama|Alabama]], Stutz packed his bags for [[Tuscaloosa, Alabama|Tuscaloosa]]

==College career==

He redshirted at [[University of Alabama|Alabama]]. In 2002, he played one game with the [[Alabama Crimson Tide|Crimson Tide]] for Franchione. When Franchione accepted the head coach position at [[Texas A&M Aggies|Texas A&M]], Stutz followed him to [[College Station, Texas|College Station]] and enrolled at A&M in the fall. Stutz sat out the football season per [[NCAA]] transfer rules. He had a solid 2004 season at Texas A&M, starting eight games at tight end in playing in all 12 of the Aggies games as a deep snapper and on [[special teams]]. Had 11 catches for 142 yards and one touchdown. Nine of his catches produced first downs. Had a career-best four catches for 49 yards against [[Clemson University|Clemson]].

In 2005, he became the team's full-time deep snapper, playing in all 12 of the Aggies' games in that capacity and started two games at tight end, making two catches for 26 yards and a touchdown. He also caught a 7-yard touchdown pass in the Magnolia Gridiron All-Star Classic – a postseason all-star game.

==Professional career==

===2006 season===

He was originally signed as an undrafted rookie free agent with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. After being cut by the Bucs, Stutz was picked up by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] and won the starting long snapping job. He was the snapper when [[Morten Andersen]] broke the NFL career scoring record, and is featured in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

===2007 season===
On October 2, 2007 the Falcons released him. He signed with the Seahawks on October 10, 2007.

==NASCAR career==
In 2014, Stutz transitioned to [[NASCAR]], joining [[Stewart–Haas Racing]]'s [[pit stop]] development program.<ref>{{cite web|last=Andro|first=Anthony|url=http://www.foxsports.com/southwest/story/boone-stutz-nascar-pit-crew-texas-a-m-aggies-football-103114|title=Aggie Stutz making transition from football to NASCAR pit crew|work=[[Foxsports.com]]|date=October 31, 2014|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref> The following year, he became the gasman for SHR driver [[Danica Patrick]]'s No. 10 team.<ref>{{cite news|last=Hembree|first=Mike|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nascar/2015/04/09/former-nfl-player-danica-patrick-pit-crew/25542821/|title=Ex-NFL player Boone Stutz prefers pit road over gridiron|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=April 9, 2015|access-date=September 30, 2016}}</ref>
